By using 'speak();' without 'super.', you are actually calling the Dog class's overridden speak method, leading to a recursive call and eventually a stack overflow error. This distractor highlights the importance of using 'super.' to explicitly call the superclass's method. Without it, the program will not function as intended, and the dog's voice will not be correctly printed.

This distractor reverses the intended order of operations by printing 'Woof Woof!' before the dog's name. If you use this line, it would disrupt the logical flow of the output, as the superclass method already prints the name first. This distractor misrepresents the correct sequence of extending functionality in subclasses, where the subclass should add additional behavior after the superclass method has executed its part.
